Getting started with paweh

paweh package authors

Source: vignettes/paweh-01-getting-started.Rmd
paweh-01-getting-started.Rmd

Start with the recruitment decision

Suppose a team suspects that a particular DNA variant is more common in people with a disease than in people without it. They can afford to recruit 500 people in each group. Even if the difference is real, different samples will give different results. Is this budget likely to give a clear answer?

Power is the probability that the planned test will declare an association when a particular difference really exists. Minimum sample size necessary (MSSN) turns the question around: for that difference and test, how many people must the team recruit to attain its target power? Neither calculation tells us how likely the hypothesis is to be true. We must first say how large a difference is plausible and how participants will be sampled and measured.

Install and load the package

This tutorial accompanies the experimental develop branch on GitHub. To install it with the rendered articles, run the following once in R. Building the articles needs Pandoc (included with RStudio); the installation also requests the suggested R packages used in the examples.

# If needed: install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github(
  "akilanthony/paweh", ref = "develop", dependencies = TRUE,
  build_vignettes = TRUE
)

If you need only the stable package, use remotes::install_github("akilanthony/paweh", ref = "main") instead.

Then load the package in your analysis session:

library(paweh)

Read a genetic study plan

Term Meaning in this tutorial
Gene, variant, allele A gene is a stretch of DNA that provides instructions for a functional product. A variant is a difference in DNA sequence at a particular location; an allele is one version of the sequence there. A variant need not be inside a gene.
Genotype and phenotype The genotype is the pair of alleles a person carries at the location studied here. The phenotype is a measured characteristic, such as disease status or height.
Biallelic genotype: 0, 1, 2 At a location with two allele types, count copies of the allele of interest. If it is A, then aa, Aa and AA score 0, 1 and 2. Use the same allele and order in both groups.
Allele frequency The fraction of allele copies of a given type. A person with genotype Aa contributes one A out of two copies; allele frequency is different from the fraction of people carrying any A.
Disease prevalence The fraction of the source population with the disease. Recruiting equal numbers of cases and controls does not imply 50% prevalence.
Genotype relative risk Disease probability for one genotype divided by that for a reference genotype. If the probabilities are 10% and 5%, the relative risk is 2. An odds ratio compares odds (probability divided by one minus probability); it is a different input.
Mode of inheritance A rule for how disease risk changes across genotypes. Under multiplicative inheritance each additional copy multiplies risk by the same factor; under a dominant model one and two copies have the same risk.
Significance threshold and power The threshold (alpha) sets the nominal chance of a false positive when there is no association. Power is the chance of crossing the threshold when the assumed association exists.
Locus heterogeneity Different genetic locations can contribute to the same diagnosis in different people. A marker may distinguish only some of the cases from controls.
Misclassification A measured category differs from the true one: for example, recording Aa as AA (genotype error) or a truly affected person as a control (phenotype error).

Plan a case-control study from pilot frequencies

Imagine that earlier work gives the following proportions for our candidate variant. Among cases, 25% have zero copies of A, 50% have one, and 25% have two. Among controls, the corresponding proportions are 36%, 48% and 16%. Each row sums to one because every person in that group has exactly one of the three genotypes. If your pilot gives counts, divide each count by the number genotyped within its own group. Dividing by the whole pilot size answers a different question.

g_case    <- c(0.25, 0.50, 0.25)  # aa, Aa, AA among cases
g_control <- c(0.36, 0.48, 0.16)  # aa, Aa, AA among controls

With a fixed budget, what could we detect?

The frequencies describe the difference we expect in the new study. The 500 cases in the next call are people we plan to recruit, not the number of people who supplied the pilot frequencies. We assume unrelated participants, comparable source populations, and correct genotype and disease classification.

Argument Why use it here?
input_mode = "model_free" We can specify genotype frequencies separately for each group rather than deriving them from a disease model.
g1, g0 Supply the full three-element vectors for cases and controls, respectively. The 1 in g1 labels disease status; it does not mean one copy of A.
N_case = 500, k = 1 Fix the case count and the number of controls per case. Our plan has 500 controls and 1,000 participants in total.
alpha = 0.05 Use 5% for a single prespecified candidate-variant test. A scan of many variants needs a more stringent threshold to control false positives across tests.
verbose = FALSE Return the results quietly so we can display just the quantities needed for recruitment. 
fixed <- cc_power(
  N_case = 500, alpha = 0.05, k = 1, input_mode = "model_free",
  g1 = g_case, g0 = g_control, verbose = FALSE
)
c(genotype = fixed$tests$genotypes$power, trend = fixed$tests$trend$power)
##  genotype     trend 
## 0.9852151 0.9940005

The genotype test compares the whole distribution across the three categories. At these frequencies its power is 98.5%. The trend test compares mean allele-copy scores (0, 1, 2) between groups; its power is 99.4%. Here cases tend to have more copies, so the targeted trend test uses the contrast efficiently. In a different disease, one-copy carriers might stand out while both zero- and two-copy carriers have similar risks. A difference like that can be missed by a trend test. Choose the primary test for the scientific contrast before looking at study results.

If the target is 80% power, how many people are needed?

Keep the same group frequencies, threshold and allocation. Replace the fixed case count with power = 0.80. Each row below is a separate plan, depending on which test you intend to use.

needed <- cc_mssn(
  power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, k = 1, input_mode = "model_free",
  g1 = g_case, g0 = g_control, verbose = FALSE
)
g <- needed$tests$genotypes
t_plan <- needed$tests$trend
recruitment <- data.frame(
  test = c("Genotype", "Trend"),
  cases = c(g$MSSN_case, t_plan$MSSN_case),
  controls = c(g$MSSN_ctrl, t_plan$MSSN_ctrl),
  total = c(g$MSSN_total, t_plan$MSSN_total)
)
knitr::kable(recruitment)
test cases controls total
Genotype 241 241 482
Trend 197 197 394

For the genotype test, plan for 241 cases and 241 controls (482 people). For a prespecified trend test, the target is 197 cases and 197 controls (394 people). Both fit the original budget. The required counts are rounded up to whole people, so achieved power need not be exactly 80%. These targets treat the pilot proportions as the future frequencies. If the pilot was small, repeat both calls with plausible smaller differences to see whether the budget still suffices.

What if you do not have pilot frequencies?

Choose inputs based on the evidence available before recruitment:

  • Case-control, model-based: If prior studies give population prevalence (prev), disease-allele frequency (pd), and disease risk for two copies relative to zero (R2), supply those and the mode of inheritance (MOI). The model starts with Hardy–Weinberg proportions (genotype frequencies expected when allele copies pair at random) in the source population. It uses the disease risks to derive separate frequencies in cases and controls. With MOI = "M", one copy has relative risk sqrt(R2).
  • Case-control, model-free: If a comparable pilot or publication gives the group-specific distributions, supply g1 and g0 as above. No inheritance rule is required for this baseline calculation. You still assume the same allele coding, suitable sampling and a plausible contrast in the planned population. Some extensions require extra inputs; disease misclassification, for instance, also needs prevalence.
  • Affected-child trios: The transmission disequilibrium test (TDT) compares alleles passed on by parents with those not passed on. Its model-free inputs are expected transmission and non-transmission counts (ET, ENT), not case-control genotype frequencies. Counts have a scale: for power at a fixed sample size they refer to the proposed number of trios; for MSSN, supply the number of trios underlying the counts separately as n_trios. The recruitment answer is in complete families, not people.

Choose the next calculation

If your planning question is… Read next
What if only some cases carry the expected association, or genotypes or diagnoses are recorded incorrectly? Case-control design compares each requested departure separately with the same baseline. Different calling errors in cases and controls can inflate false positives; a larger nominal power then need not mean a better design.
How many families with an affected child and both parents do we need? TDT design explains transmission counts and which family-based error and heterogeneity scenarios can be modeled.
Our outcome is a measurement rather than a diagnosis. Should we measure everyone or sample extremes? Quantitative-trait design compares group means, selection from trait extremes, and designs involving several traits.
Could we explore the same assumptions without writing each call? The dashboard walkthrough connects interactive case-control, trio and quantitative-trait plans to reproducible R calls.
How does the number of reads at a variant affect recruitment? Sequencing design distinguishes case-control genotype calls from the trio method based on reads. These are fixed-depth planning models; no sequence files are needed.
Can we afford to verify diagnoses or genotypes in just part of the study? LRTae validation design allocates people according to which measurements receive a gold-standard check, and calculates power or required recruitment for that plan.

Further reading

Gordon D, Finch SJ, Kim W. Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics: How to Assess, Address, and Account for Mixtures in Association Studies. Springer; 2020. This book provides background on why mixtures matter. For the case-control error models, see Gordon et al. (2002) on genotype errors and Edwards et al. (2005) on phenotype errors. Consult the article for your design for its specific method and assumptions. Use citation("paweh") for the software citation.

For other planning questions, Quanto includes gene–gene and gene–environment interaction designs. Michigan’s CaTS supports large association studies including two-stage designs, and its GAS calculator provides a related one-stage power calculation.
